name: money
intent: Represent an amount of money as one immutable value that carries its currency and owns the rounding, allocation and conversion rules, so that money arithmetic can never silently mix units or lose minor units to binary floating point.
problem: Amounts are handled as bare numbers in binary floating point: rounding happens wherever it is convenient, a currency's minor unit is assumed to be two, splitting an amount by division loses or invents minor units, and adding two different currencies yields a plausible-looking number instead of an error.
context: Application and domain code that prices, bills, pays, taxes, converts or splits money - multi-currency commerce, invoicing, payroll, ledgers and payment flows - and every boundary (database column, API payload, message, spreadsheet export) that an amount has to cross without changing value. It applies whenever currency and rounding policy are part of the amount's meaning rather than only of its presentation.
benefits: Units cannot be lost: arithmetic on two different currencies fails loudly instead of silently adding dollars to yen.
Exactness end to end: with an exact decimal or an integer count of minor units, amounts survive input, storage, aggregation and serialization without binary rounding drift.
One owner for rounding and currency rules: the minor-unit exponent, the rounding mode and cash rounding live in the value, not in scattered call sites.
Allocation that conserves the total: percentages, instalments, discounts and tax splits are distributed so the parts always sum to the whole, with no lost pennies.
Self-documenting signatures: an amount parameter carries its currency, so the compiler - or a cheap check at construction - rejects the mistake at the source instead of during reconciliation.

A single place to parse, format and serialize, which turns the wire format into a deliberate decision (minor-unit integer or decimal string) instead of a JSON number that every parser reads as a double.
tradeoffs: Exact arithmetic is slower and allocates: BigDecimal, rust_decimal, Python Decimal and BigInt are far heavier than double, so high-volume paths fall back to fixed-scale integers and accept a precision ceiling.

The currency has to travel with the amount through every layer - table columns, DTOs, messages, metrics - and one leak (a JSON number, a float column, a spreadsheet) reintroduces exactly the bug the pattern removes.

Rounding does not disappear, it becomes an explicit policy: per-line versus document-level tax, half-even versus half-up where a regulator demands it, and a rounded total that may legitimately differ from the sum of rounded lines.

Division has to be replaced by allocation with a leftover-distribution policy, which is custom code and a design decision (largest remainder, round-robin, nearest) that a plain amount / n never forced.

Interoperability friction when implementations meet: two money types with the same amount and currency need not be equal (JSR 354 includes the implementation type in equals), so conversion at the boundary is real work.
Currency metadata rots: ISO 4217 exponents are not uniformly two (JPY has none, BHD and KWD have three), redenominations happen, and a hard-coded exponent or symbol table will eventually be wrong.
Persistence and serialization need dedicated converters in every mapping layer (ORM type handler, JSON, XML, CSV), because the value is deliberately not a primitive.

participants.responsibility: Immutable value combining amount and currency; owns equality, comparison, closed arithmetic, rounding and allocation, and refuses operations that would mix currencies.
The exact numeric representation: an integer count of minor units or an arbitrary-precision decimal, never a binary floating-point number.
ISO 4217 identity of the unit, carrying the minor-unit exponent and the formatting and cash-rounding metadata that every rounding decision needs.
The explicit mode and scale (half-even, half-up, cash rounding) applied once, at the point where money is settled, allocated or converted.
Distributes an amount over ratios or n targets and hands out the remaining minor units so the parts sum exactly to the original amount.
Applies an exchange rate of a known scale and timestamp, performs the single rounding step into the target currency, and returns a new amount instead of mutating one.
Turns an exact amount into a localized string for humans; lives outside the value and never feeds parsed display text back into arithmetic.

use_cases: Checkout and order totals: line items priced in different currencies, shipping and tax, with the order total allocated from the sum of rounded lines.
Invoicing and tax: per-line versus document-level VAT with a declared rounding mode, matching an e-invoicing validator's expectation that the lines sum to the total.
Ledgers and payments: debit and credit postings in minor units, reconciled against a bank or processor that speaks integer minor units.
Payroll and multi-currency payouts: converting a salary into the recipient's currency with a dated rate and a single rounding step.
Instalments, subscriptions and proration: splitting an amount across n periods, or refunding part of a period, without losing a minor unit.
Reporting and reconciliation: aggregating exact amounts across services that exchange money as decimal strings or minor-unit integers.
Java monetary services: JavaMoney (JSR 354) and its Moneta reference implementation provide currency-aware amounts, rounding, conversion and formatting for billing, settlement and exchange.
.NET billing and payments: NodaMoney's Money, FastMoney and Currency types keep amounts currency-aware while offering decimal and fixed-scale performance paths.
Ruby commerce and invoicing: RubyMoney's Money object stores integer subunits with currency metadata and provides arithmetic, exchange and rounding APIs.
avoid_when: The data is a count rather than money: loyalty points, tokens or unit counts want a Newtype over an integer, not a currency and a rounding policy.
Only presentation is at stake: a layer that never does arithmetic and never rounds, just rendering a number produced elsewhere, needs a locale formatter and nothing more.
Every amount lives in one currency and arrives and leaves as integer minor units with database constraints; a named integer type plus the naming convention suffices.
The system is an exploratory script or an analysis whose output is never reconciled against a ledger and whose errors below the minor unit are irrelevant.
A payment processor or ERP already owns amounts as minor-unit integers and defines the contract: model its wire type instead of re-modelling money locally.
anti_patterns: Money as a float or double, introduced 'temporarily', producing one-minor-unit reconciliation gaps that only surface in production data.
An amount column or parameter with no currency beside it (or a Money type whose currency lives in a comment), so the unit exists only in tribal knowledge.
Rounding the unit price first and multiplying afterwards: $0.0034 rounds to $0.00 and a 100,000-unit order becomes free - the canonical bulk-pricing bug.
Splitting an amount by dividing and rounding each share, after which the parts no longer sum to the whole.
Storing or transmitting money as a JSON number, which mainstream parsers convert to an IEEE-754 double at the door.
A Money type that permits cross-currency addition 'because the rate is applied elsewhere', or a mutable global exchange rate.
Parsing amounts out of locale-formatted display strings ('1.234,56'), so display and data are no longer separable.
design_principles: Single responsibility: one owner of currency identity, minor units and rounding policy.
Make illegal states unrepresentable: currency is part of the value, so cross-currency addition is a type error or a loud exception.
Immutability and value semantics: equals and hashCode over amount plus currency, no setters, safe as a map key and across threads.
Information hiding: the minor-unit exponent and the rounding mode live behind the currency, not in caller arithmetic.
Closure of operations: arithmetic on money yields money, so expressions stay in the domain instead of collapsing to bare numbers.
Separation of concerns: computation, rounding policy, allocation and locale formatting are distinct and independently testable.
best_practices: Store the amount as an integer count of minor units or an exact decimal; never a binary float, not even transiently in a mapping layer.
Keep the currency attached to every representation of an amount - database columns, DTOs, events, logs - and validate the ISO code at construction.
Look the minor-unit exponent up per currency instead of assuming two decimals; treat the exponent as data.
Cross the wire as integer minor units or a decimal string, and make that choice explicit in the serializer.
Round once, explicitly, where money is settled, allocated or converted; pass the mode as a parameter rather than relying on a hidden default.
Use allocation (largest remainder or another documented leftover strategy) instead of division for splits, percentages and tax distribution.
Keep locale-specific symbols and formatting in the presentation layer, and exchange rates in their own operation carrying rate, timestamp and rounding.
Test the invariants, not only examples: parts sum to the whole, addition is associative and commutative, and parse/format round-trips exactly.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Base Patterns chapter: Money (with Quantity).
